title: Chapter 138 – The Orchard Below
html:
[The Lin Orchard – Lin Jian]

At sixty, Purple Mansion Late comes to him quietly, like a lamp lit in the next room.

There is no pill. There is no cocoon. He is sitting on the Dock stair at dusk, with a bowl of cold barley porridge in his lap, when he feels something shift in the soles of his feet. A faint pressure. A turn of a key. He looks down at his hands and they are the same hands, scarred and white-knuckled and old, but the air around them has thickened, as though the world had leaned a hair's breadth closer to listen.

```
BREAKTHROUGH COMPLETE — PURPLE MANSION LATE
Qi 11 Body 10 Soul 10
Age: 60
Seal: 63% (+3 from rest)
Note: The Chain nights built your Soul. The Chain
would have you pay for it. Counted: 96 nights.
Reservoir: 171 / 200
```

Ninety-six nights. He does the arithmetic without effort. Eight years of the last moon, a hundred hours of lying on cold jade among thirty sleepers, breathing their rhythm, lending them his breath. He had thought it a duty. He had not thought of it as a school.

He finishes the porridge. He sits for a while longer in the dark, listening to the stair hum under him, and then he goes in to tell his mother.

She is at the stove. She does not turn.

"Late," she says.

"How did you know?"

"You walk louder." She stirs the pot. "Your father is on the porch with a face like a hen. Go and tell him. Then tell me where you are going."

He stops in the doorway.

"I have not said I am going anywhere."

"You have the look." She sets down the spoon. She is eighty-four, and she has the face of a woman of forty-five, and there is something very old in her eyes. "The Gate stirred last night. Feng heard it. Yue heard it. I did not need to. I felt it in my teeth." She turns. "Where?"

"The Orchard," says Jian.

The kitchen is quiet.

"I had thought it might be," says Qinghe.

* * *

Wenyuan will not be left behind.

He says so at the table, to the room at large, with his gloved hands folded on the cloth. He is eighty-six. He has the thin careful voice of a very old man, and the eyes of a boy. "I was born in that place. I buried my mother in it. I carried a basket of eggs down its main road to a girl in a blue skirt." He nods at Qinghe, who is studying the ceiling. "I have not seen it in sixty years. I will see it before I die."

"Father, you will not die."

"Then I will see it before I do not." He smiles. "I am a Foundation Establishment Middle. I can walk a hundred li on a good day. If I fall behind, you may carry me. You carried me, once. I remember."

It is a joke. It is also not. Jian looks at the old face, at the cold hands, at the grave steady brown eyes, and finds that there is no argument.

They set out three days later, at dawn: Jian, Wenyuan, Yue, and Pebble. Qinghe sees them off at the Garden gate with a bundle of travel bread and a stern look. She is not coming. She has, she says, a pot to mind, and a granddaughter who has been caught reading the ledger of doors under the bed. But when Wenyuan bends to kiss her, she takes his cold face in both her hands and holds it a moment, and says nothing at all.

The Unkept follow at forty paces. There are nine of them now. Lan Wen, with his white eye, is at the head.

* * *

It takes four days, on foot, through country that Jian has never seen.

The road runs north and west from the Garden, up into a high bare country of limestone and scrub. The villages thin. The trees dwindle to thorn and juniper. On the second night they camp under an overhang of gray rock, and Wenyuan sits by the fire with his knees pulled up, and tells them about the Orchard.

He tells it slowly, in the voice of a man who is surprised to find that the words are still there. Two hundred acres of apple. A square stone house with a slate roof. A well. A cider press. A road of white gravel lined with poplars, and a gate with a lantern on a bracket. A family of fifty. A feast-day every autumn, when the whole of it was laid out under the trees on trestle tables and everybody ate until they burst.

"It was a happy place," he says. "I did not know it. One does not."

"What happened to it?" asks Yue.

"The Registry." He says it flatly. "I was twenty-six. A clerk came in the spring with a letter, and read out a decree that the Orchard was forfeit. The old men argued. The clerk smiled. The next morning, there were fifty riders at the gate." He stirs the fire with a stick. "My father did not wish to run. He said it was his land. They burned the house with him in it."

Yue's hand goes to her mouth.

"We took what we could carry. We walked for eleven days. I carried your mother's trunk." A faint smile, brief and painful. "She was my wife, then, and heavy with Jian. Feng was six and rode on the trunk. She walked every step. She said, I do not wish to be anywhere else."

Nobody says anything. The fire cracks. Pebble, on Yue's knee, has her ears flat.

"The thing I never understood," says Wenyuan, "is why. We were farmers. We had no wealth. We had no power. There was nothing under that land but chalk and roots." He looks up, and his eyes in the firelight are bright. "They burned it like a man stamping on a nest."

Jian says nothing. He is watching Pebble.

She is listening to the ground.

* * *

On the third night, Wenyuan tells the other story, the one that was never told to children.

They are camped in a dry gully with a fire of thorn and a pot of rice, and the stars are out hard and close. Yue has gone to sleep with her head on her pack. Pebble sits upright on a rock with her tail around her feet. Jian is cleaning a bowl with a handful of sand. Wenyuan watches the coals for a long time.

"My grandfather told it to me when I was nine," he says. "He said I was to keep it. He said a time would come when somebody asked."

"Asked what?"

"Where the Lin came from." The old man's voice is soft. "We were not always the Lin. That is a Sect name, a registry name, something a clerk wrote in a book when my great-grandfather needed a license. Before that we were nobody. A family of laborers, from the south, walking north in a bad year. They came to the valley with a cart and a sick child and nothing else."

"And?"

"There was a man waiting." Wenyuan lifts his eyes. "At the crossroads. A tall man in a blue smock, with spectacles, who looked like nothing any of them had ever seen. He was sitting on a rock eating an apple. He said, 'You look hungry.'"

Jian's hands have stopped on the bowl.

"He gave them the apple. He said he had been there a long time. He said there was a good piece of land, a few miles on, if they cared to work it. He walked them to it. He showed them where to plant. He gave them a seedling, a single seedling in a clay pot, and told them that it was theirs, but that they would have to promise one thing." The fire pops. "That they would never let it die."

"What happened to him?"

"My grandfather did not know. He said the man stayed three seasons. He taught them to graft. He taught them to read. He sat on a stool at the edge of the field in the evenings and talked to the tree." Wenyuan smiles faintly. "One day he walked off down the road, and did not come back. But the Lin kept the promise. Seven generations. We never let it die."

"What was his name?"

"They called him the Stranger." The old man shrugs. "My grandfather said he had a scar on his left palm. And that when the children asked him where he came from, he would only say, a long way back. And a long way forward."

Nobody speaks. A breeze lifts the ash.

"I thought it a tale," says Wenyuan. "A thing to make children behave. I did not think of it again for fifty years." He turns his cold gloved hands over. "And then you were born, and looked at the lamp, and I thought of the blue smock. I do not know why. I only know that I did."

Jian puts down the bowl. He cannot look at his father.

"Father," he says quietly. "What color was your eyes?"

"My eyes?" The old man laughs. "Brown, boy. As they have always been. Why?"

"No reason."

It is not true. He has remembered something he thought he had forgotten. A small boy, sitting on a stool beside a bed, looking at a lamp, and thinking, the man in the blue smock is coming.

He does not know whose memory it is.

* * *

On the fourth day, in the late afternoon, they come over a low ridge and see it.

It is nothing. That is the first shock. It is a long shallow valley of pale grass, ringed with dry hills, under a pale high sky, and in the grass, here and there, are low gray humps of stone. A line of broken poplars marks the road. The orchard itself is gone, a plain of coarse yellow meadow, rippling in the wind, with only the rotted stumps of a few thousand trees showing like teeth.

Wenyuan stops.

He stands at the top of the ridge with his hand on the staff Qinghe packed for him, and says nothing, for a very long time. The wind blows his silver hair. His face, in profile, is old and calm and perfectly blank.

"There," he says at last.

He points. In the center of the valley, a little apart from the humps of the foundations, stands a single tree.

It is an apple. It is old, crooked, enormous, black with age. Its trunk is twice the girth of a man. Its branches are bare, for it is autumn, but it is hung with red, a few dozen small hard fruit clinging to the twigs like drops of blood. It stands alone in a wide ring of bare earth, as though the grass had refused to come near it. It is the only living thing on the plain.

"That was my grandfather's," says Wenyuan. "The first. They called it the Mother. Nobody was allowed to pick from it." He swallows. "I had thought it burned."

"It did not," says Pebble.

She has leapt to the ground. She stands rigid in the grass with her ears pricked and every hair on end, staring at the tree, and her voice when it comes is thin and very high.

"It is all here," she says. "The whole field. Every seam I have been hearing for twenty years, they all point to that." Her eyes are huge. "It is the center. It is the root of the world."

* * *

Wenyuan finds his mother's grave before they go down, and it takes him an hour.

The graveyard lies on a low rise at the west edge of the valley, a plot of perhaps two hundred small mounds, long since leveled by weather, with a few leaning slate markers still upright. He walks among them with Yue at his elbow, bent double, reading the stones. Some are nameless. Some have been worn smooth by fifty winters of rain. At the far corner, under a tangle of dead bramble, he finds one that is neither, and stops.

Lin Ah-Mei, it says. Beloved.

That is all. Wenyuan lowers himself to his knees in the dry grass with a grunt, and takes off one glove, and lays his bare cold palm against the stone.

"Mother," he says.

Yue turns away. She stands at a polite distance with her back to him and her arms folded, watching the sky, and Pebble sits at her feet. Jian, on the path, does not move. The wind carries the old man's voice to them in pieces.

"...I have a son. Two. And a daughter. They are well. The little one turned out to be a great man. You would not believe it. He is very tall and gray and does not eat enough..." A pause. "...your daughter-in-law is a wonder. She makes a terrible rice. I would not change it..."

The grass hisses. A crow lands on a marker, looks at them, and flies off.

"...I did not come sooner. I am sorry. I was afraid there would be nothing. I find there is a stone." His voice cracks. "That is more than most."

He is quiet for a long time.

When he rises it takes Yue and Jian both to help him. His knees are green and his face is wet. He is smiling.

"She said I was a fool to leave a good job at the mill for farming," he tells them cheerfully. "She was right. I have never regretted it."

He walks down the slope with his staff, a little ahead of them, and they follow at a distance and say nothing. Jian lingers a moment at the corner stone, and, because he has nothing else to give, takes the small wooden spoon from his breast and lays it, briefly, on the grass beside the name, and then picks it up again. It is a foolish gesture. He feels better for it. On the far side of the valley, the Mother Tree has begun to glow with a faint reddish light in the failing sun, as though it had been waiting for them to look.

They go down in the last light.

The grass is waist-high and dry as paper. The foundations are small low squares of fieldstone, half sunk in the earth, with here and there a doorstep, a hearth, a well-curb with the bucket-chain rusted solid. Wenyuan walks among them in silence, touching things. A broken millstone. A black iron hook. The handle of a plow. He kneels at one hearth and picks up a handful of ash and lets it run through his fingers, and nobody says a word.

At the foot of the Mother Tree, they stop.

Close to, it is even larger than it looked. The bark is deeply furrowed, black and silver, like the skin of an ancient animal. The roots break the surface of the ground in great knotted ridges, and the earth between them is baked hard. The fruit is just out of reach. A single red apple hangs, perfect, in the evening light, level with Jian's eyes.

He looks at it for a long time.

"May I?" he asks.

Wenyuan stares. "You may," he says. "You are the grandson."

Jian reaches up. The stem is thick and woody. When he closes his hand around the fruit it comes away with a soft crack, and it is cold, very cold, like a stone from a spring. He turns it over. It is the size of a plum, glossy red, flawless. He lifts it to his nose.

It smells of nothing.

"Do not eat it," says Pebble.

"I wasn't going to."

"There is a seam in the core." She is shivering. "A big one. It goes down."

He cuts the apple in half with his thumbnail. The flesh is white. In the very center of it, where the seeds should be, there is a tiny hole, round and clean and black, no larger than a pinhead. Looking into it is like looking down a well that has no bottom. A faint wind rises from it, smelling of iron.

"Show me," he says.

* * *

They find the door at the foot of the Mother Tree, on the north side, between two roots, under a mat of rotted leaves.

It is a slab of green stone, set flush with the earth, no larger than a cart-bed, and as smooth as glass. There is no handle. There is no lock. There is only, in the center, an indentation the size of a man's palm, rimmed with a fine pattern of lines. Jian kneels in the leaf mold and brushes it clean. His hands are not quite steady.

"It is the Gate," says Yue softly. "The same stone. But so much older."

"It is the first." He lays his palm in the hollow. "The very first."

The stone is warm.

It is the warmth of a living thing, a faint steady pulse, like the flank of a sleeping horse. He feels it come up into his wrist and along his arm, and a panel unfolds in his sight, calm and clean.

```
DOCK — ARK-1 (origin site)
Status: DORMANT (not dark)
Wake: none required.
Note: This site has been awake the whole time.
It was waiting for the eighth.
Access: Operator (8th) + 2 witnesses, unarmed.
Witnesses present: LIN WENYUAN, LIN YUE.
Beast PEBBLE: permitted.
```

He reads it, and swallows.

"Two witnesses," he says. "It wants you both. You are to go in with me."

Wenyuan looks at him. He is white. He is leaning on the staff. "I am a farmer," he says, in a small voice. "I am eighty-six. I do not know a thing about doors."

"You know the Orchard." Jian rises. He holds out his hand. "Come."

Behind them, at the rim of the ring of bare earth, the Unkept have stopped. Lan Wen has raised one hand, and the eight others have halted in a row, gray and silent in the dusk. They will not cross the line where the grass gives way to dirt. Lan Wen bows, very low, and does not speak.

"We guard the outside," he says, at last, in his rusty voice. "As we have always done. We will be here."

The old man hesitates. Then, with the grave dignity of a man stepping onto a boat, he takes the hand, and lets himself be drawn forward onto the green stone. The slab sinks beneath their feet with a long soft sigh. Yue steps on after, with Pebble in her arms. And the three of them go down together into the dark, through the roots of the Mother Tree, as the wind rises in the dead grass and the last light fails.

* * *

It is not a room. It is a hall.

He understands, when the lights come up, that it is the largest Dock he has seen: a long white cavern, as wide as a barn, with a vaulted ceiling and a polished floor, lined on both sides with tall green pillars, each carved with a different fruit. Apple. Pear. Plum. Cherry. They go away into the distance in two glowing rows, like the aisle of a cathedral. At the far end, on a low dais, stands a single stool, and on the stool a plain gray box.

It is an ugly thing. It is the size of a loaf of bread, made of dull metal, with a grill on its face and a single small round button on top. A scrap of white paper is taped to the front. There is a rust stain on one corner.

They walk toward it in silence. Their footsteps ring.

Wenyuan stops at the foot of the dais. He is shaking. "What is it?"

"I think," says Jian slowly, "that it is a voice."

The paper on the box has a line of text in blue ink.

Press here. You've been waiting long enough.

He puts out his hand. Beside him, Yue has caught her breath. Pebble is utterly still. The great hall hums, a long low note, and Jian presses the button.

* * *

There is a click. A hiss like rain on tin. A sound he has not heard in sixty years, and has never forgotten.

A chair creaking. A cup set down.

Then a man clears his throat.

"Okay," says a voice. "Okay. Is this on? It says it's on."

It is a tired voice. It is low and dry and a little hoarse, with a slight rasp, as of someone who has been talking for hours. It speaks in the plain flat accent of a man from a place that has no name here, and every vowel of it is a pang. Jian's knees nearly go. He has not heard that accent since the hospital. He has not heard it in any language, in any voice, in the whole of his life as Lin Jian.

"This is Ethan Cole," says the voice. "The original. The first one. I'm recording this in a room I built myself, in a world I can't see out of, for a person I won't meet." A dry cough. "Which is a hell of a thing to say into a box. I'm sorry. I've been rehearsing it for three weeks and it still sounds stupid."

Yue has taken Wenyuan's arm. The old man is staring at the box as if it were an open grave.

"I'm going to say this plainly," says Ethan Cole, "because I've learned I'm bad at saying it any other way. If you're hearing this, you're the eighth. Which means it's worked. Which means I'm either very lucky or very stupid, and I haven't decided which."

A pause. A long breath.

"You've been reading my letters," says the voice, more gently. "The little ones. In the Docks. They're not from me. I mean, they are, but they're from the other me. The ones who forgot. I didn't write them, not exactly. I mean I wrote them after. Each time. Once I'd been restored. I wrote each one fresh, and had it carried here, to the front, so the next one could find it." Another breath. "It's a hell of a postal system. Believe me. I've thought about it."

He laughs, a short helpless sound.

"I should tell you the thing you've been trying to find out. I know you have. I've watched every one of you try. It's the same question every time. Why? Why the Docks, why the Gate, why the Order, why the loop. Why a man should be sent into a world not his own, over and over, to forget himself and be forgotten and be fetched back by people who love him." His voice drops. "I can't tell you why. I'm sorry. It isn't safe to say it here. They're listening. They always are. But I can tell you who."

The light in the great hall seems to thicken. Jian does not breathe.

"There's no Order," says Ethan Cole. "Not really. No Registry, no Keepers, no Houses. They're just what happens when you leave a man alone with a problem for six hundred years. They think they're serving me. They're not. They're serving him."

"Him," whispers Yue.

"The first one," says the voice. "The one who started it. The one who built the Gate and the Docks and the Chain, and gave the Order its first task, and told them to wait." A silence, in which the hiss of the tape is very loud. "I need you to understand something, kid. Because I'm going to say it once, and you're going to hate me for it, and you're going to be right."

"The first one," says Ethan Cole, "was me."

"I built the loop."
